entities.name: Blue whale
entities.fact: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, reaching about 30 metres and well over 150 tonnes.

entities.name: Humpback whale
entities.fact: Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs, and the scientific name Megaptera novaeangliae means 'big-winged New Englander'.

entities.name: Fin whale
entities.fact: The fin whale is the second-largest animal and has odd asymmetric colouring, with a white lower right jaw and a dark left one.

entities.name: Sei whale
entities.fact: The sei whale is one of the fastest great whales and was hunted hard in the 1960s once fin whale numbers had collapsed.

entities.name: Bryde's whale
entities.fact: Bryde's whale is named after Johan Bryde, a Norwegian who set up South Africa's first whaling stations, and it stays in warm waters all year.

entities.name: Minke whale
entities.fact: Minke whales are the smallest of the rorquals and the main target of whaling by Norway, Japan and Iceland today.

entities.name: Antarctic minke whale
entities.fact: Antarctic minke whales live among the pack ice and were the main target of Japan's so-called scientific whaling in the Southern Ocean.

entities.name: Gray whale
entities.fact: Gray whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, up to about 20,000 kilometres a year between Mexico and the Arctic.

entities.name: Bowhead whale
entities.fact: Bowhead whales can live more than 200 years and use their huge heads to break through sea ice.

entities.name: Right whale
entities.fact: Right whales got their name from whalers because they were the 'right' whale to hunt: slow, rich in oil, and floating when dead.

entities.name: North Atlantic right whale
entities.fact: The North Atlantic right whale is one of the most endangered great whales, with only around 370 left off eastern North America.

entities.name: Southern right whale
entities.fact: Southern right whales 'sail' by holding their tail flukes up in the wind, and they gather to calve off Argentina, South Africa and Australia.

entities.name: North Pacific right whale
entities.fact: The North Pacific right whale is one of the rarest whales, with perhaps only about 30 animals left in the eastern North Pacific.

entities.name: Sperm whale
entities.fact: Sperm whales dive over 2 kilometres deep hunting squid and have the largest brain of any animal.

entities.name: Pygmy sperm whale
entities.fact: The pygmy sperm whale squirts a cloud of reddish-brown fluid to confuse predators, much as a squid uses ink.

entities.name: Dwarf sperm whale
entities.fact: The dwarf sperm whale is the smallest animal commonly called a whale, at about 2.7 metres long, and releases a cloud of dark fluid when alarmed.

entities.name: Beluga whale
entities.fact: Belugas are nicknamed sea canaries for their chirps and whistles, and they can turn their heads because their neck bones are not fused.

entities.name: Narwhal
entities.fact: The narwhal's spiral tusk is actually a tooth that can grow to about 3 metres and is packed with nerve endings.

entities.name: Orca
entities.fact: Orcas are actually the largest dolphins, and different populations have their own dialects and hunting traditions.

entities.name: Pilot whale
entities.fact: Pilot whales are large dolphins that travel in tight-knit pods and are prone to mass strandings on beaches.

entities.name: Long-finned pilot whale
entities.fact: Long-finned pilot whales are the target of the Faroe Islands' drive hunt, and their pods follow a leader so closely that they strand together.

entities.name: Short-finned pilot whale
entities.fact: Short-finned pilot whales sprint after squid in the deep, earning the nickname 'cheetahs of the deep', and females live decades past menopause.

entities.name: False killer whale
entities.fact: False killer whales are large dark dolphins known for sharing prey with each other and for hunting alongside bottlenose dolphins.

entities.name: Pygmy killer whale
entities.fact: The pygmy killer whale is a small, little-known dark dolphin of tropical seas that was known only from two skulls until the 1950s.

entities.name: Melon-headed whale
entities.fact: Melon-headed whales travel in pods of hundreds and are actually dolphins, despite their name.

entities.name: Beaked whale
entities.fact: Beaked whales are deep-diving, elusive whales with just one or two pairs of teeth, and some species are known only from stranded animals.

entities.name: Cuvier's beaked whale
entities.fact: Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal diving records, with dives to nearly 3,000 metres and lasting over three hours.

entities.name: Blainville's beaked whale
entities.fact: Blainville's beaked whale has the densest bone known in any animal, in its beak, and is named after French zoologist Henri de Blainville.

entities.name: Baird's beaked whale
entities.fact: Baird's beaked whale is the largest beaked whale, up to about 13 metres, and is still hunted off Japan in small numbers.

entities.name: Sowerby's beaked whale
entities.fact: Sowerby's beaked whale was the first beaked whale described, from an animal stranded in the Moray Firth in Scotland in 1800.

entities.name: True's beaked whale
entities.fact: True's beaked whale is named after Frederick True, an American museum curator, and was first filmed underwater in the Azores in 2017.

entities.name: Gervais' beaked whale
entities.fact: Gervais' beaked whale lives in the deep Atlantic and was first described from a carcass found floating in the English Channel in 1840.

entities.name: Gray's beaked whale
entities.fact: Gray's beaked whale, named after British zoologist John Edward Gray, is the beaked whale most often stranded in New Zealand and is seen in cold Southern Ocean waters.

entities.name: Strap-toothed whale
entities.fact: Male strap-toothed whales, also called Layard's beaked whales, grow two tusks that curl over the upper jaw and stop the mouth opening more than a few centimetres.

entities.name: Northern bottlenose whale
entities.fact: Northern bottlenose whales were heavily hunted in the North Atlantic for their oil and are famously curious about boats.

entities.name: Southern bottlenose whale
entities.fact: The southern bottlenose whale feeds near the Antarctic ice edge and is one of the most often sighted beaked whales in the Southern Ocean.

entities.name: Arnoux's beaked whale
entities.fact: Arnoux's beaked whale lives in the cold Southern Ocean and has been seen diving beneath Antarctic sea ice.

entities.name: Shepherd's beaked whale
entities.fact: Shepherd's beaked whale is the only beaked whale with a full set of functional teeth in both jaws.

entities.name: Stejneger's beaked whale
entities.fact: Stejneger's beaked whale, also called the Bering Sea beaked whale, lives in cold North Pacific waters and often strands in the Aleutian Islands.

entities.name: Hubbs' beaked whale
entities.fact: Hubbs' beaked whale is known mostly from strandings on the US west coast and Japan, and males carry a white cap on their heads.

entities.name: Longman's beaked whale
entities.fact: Longman's beaked whale was known only from two skulls for most of the 20th century and lives in warm Indo-Pacific waters.

entities.name: Hector's beaked whale
entities.fact: Hector's beaked whale is a small, rarely seen Southern Hemisphere beaked whale named after James Hector, a New Zealand scientist.

entities.name: Andrews' beaked whale
entities.fact: Andrews' beaked whale is known almost entirely from strandings in Australia and New Zealand and is named after explorer Roy Chapman Andrews.

entities.name: Spade-toothed whale
entities.fact: The spade-toothed whale is the rarest whale known; only a handful of specimens have ever been found, and none has been seen alive at sea.

entities.name: Ramari's beaked whale
entities.fact: Ramari's beaked whale, described in 2021, is named after Māori whale expert Ramari Stewart, the first cetacean named after an indigenous woman.

entities.name: Omura's whale
entities.fact: Omura's whale was only recognised as a species in 2003 and was first filmed alive off Madagascar in 2015.

entities.name: Rice's whale
entities.fact: Rice's whale, named in 2021 after biologist Dale Rice, lives only in the Gulf of Mexico and numbers only around 50 animals.

entities.name: Pygmy right whale
entities.fact: The pygmy right whale is the smallest and least-known baleen whale, rarely seen alive in the cool waters of the Southern Hemisphere.

entities.name: Dolphin
entities.fact: Dolphins are toothed whales with cone-shaped teeth and a beak, and they hunt using echolocation clicks.

entities.name: Porpoise
entities.fact: Porpoises are small toothed whales with spade-shaped teeth and blunt snouts, unlike the cone-shaped teeth and beaks of dolphins.

entities.name: Bottlenose dolphin
entities.fact: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by name using signature whistles that each dolphin invents as a calf.

entities.name: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin
entities.fact: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia, carry sponges on their beaks as tools to protect them while foraging on the seabed.

entities.name: Common dolphin
entities.fact: Common dolphins have a bold hourglass pattern on their sides and gather in superpods of thousands.

entities.name: Long-beaked common dolphin
entities.fact: The long-beaked common dolphin hugs the coasts of California, Peru and West Africa and has a noticeably longer snout than its short-beaked cousin.

entities.name: Spinner dolphin
entities.fact: Spinner dolphins leap and spin several times in the air, and rest in shallow bays by day after hunting offshore at night.

entities.name: Striped dolphin
entities.fact: Striped dolphins are fast, acrobatic dolphins with blue-black stripes and are the most common dolphin in the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Risso's dolphin
entities.fact: Risso's dolphins are born dark grey and turn almost white with age as they accumulate scars from fights and squid.

entities.name: Dusky dolphin
entities.fact: Dusky dolphins of New Zealand, South Africa and South America are famous for high, acrobatic leaps and somersaults.

entities.name: Pacific white-sided dolphin
entities.fact: Pacific white-sided dolphins travel in boisterous groups of hundreds in the cool North Pacific and often ride the bow waves of ships.

entities.name: Atlantic white-sided dolphin
entities.fact: The Atlantic white-sided dolphin has a bold yellow-ochre streak on its tail stock and lives in cool North Atlantic waters.

entities.name: White-beaked dolphin
entities.fact: The white-beaked dolphin is a robust cold-water dolphin that ranges north into Arctic waters off Greenland, Svalbard and Norway.

entities.name: Atlantic spotted dolphin
entities.fact: Atlantic spotted dolphins are born spotless and gain more spots with age, and the Bahamas population has been studied for over 30 years.

entities.name: Pantropical spotted dolphin
entities.fact: Pantropical spotted dolphins swim above yellowfin tuna in the eastern Pacific, where millions died in tuna nets before dolphin-safe fishing.

entities.name: Clymene dolphin
entities.fact: The Clymene dolphin of the Atlantic is the only marine mammal known to have arisen as a hybrid, from spinner and striped dolphins.

entities.name: Hector's dolphin
entities.fact: Hector's dolphin of New Zealand is one of the smallest dolphins, about 1.4 metres long, with a rounded dorsal fin like a Mickey Mouse ear.

entities.name: Māui dolphin
entities.fact: The Māui dolphin, a subspecies of Hector's dolphin off New Zealand's North Island, is among the rarest dolphins with only around 50 adults left.

entities.name: Commerson's dolphin
entities.fact: Commerson's dolphin, with its black-and-white panda colouring, lives off Patagonia and, oddly, in the far-off Kerguelen Islands.

entities.name: Heaviside's dolphin
entities.fact: Heaviside's dolphin, found only off Namibia and South Africa, carries the misspelled name of a ship's captain who brought a specimen to Britain.

entities.name: Chilean dolphin
entities.fact: The Chilean dolphin is a small, shy dolphin of Chile's fjords, channels and estuaries and is found nowhere else.

entities.name: Peale's dolphin
entities.fact: Peale's dolphin lives among the kelp beds and channels of Patagonia and the Falkland Islands and is named after artist Titian Peale.

entities.name: Fraser's dolphin
entities.fact: Fraser's dolphin was described in 1956 from a skeleton found in Sarawak and was not seen alive by scientists until the 1970s.

entities.name: Rough-toothed dolphin
entities.fact: The rough-toothed dolphin has a sloping, reptile-like head with no crease between beak and forehead, and finely ridged teeth.

entities.name: Hourglass dolphin
entities.fact: The hourglass dolphin is the only small dolphin found regularly in Antarctic waters, and its bold black-and-white pattern gives it its name.

entities.name: Southern right whale dolphin
entities.fact: The southern right whale dolphin has no dorsal fin at all and is strikingly black and white.

entities.name: Northern right whale dolphin
entities.fact: The northern right whale dolphin of the North Pacific has no dorsal fin and skims along the surface in low, long leaps.

entities.name: Irrawaddy dolphin
entities.fact: Irrawaddy dolphins in Myanmar herd fish towards fishermen's nets and are rewarded with part of the catch.

entities.name: Australian snubfin dolphin
entities.fact: The Australian snubfin dolphin was only recognised as a species in 2005 and spits water to herd fish in northern Australia's estuaries.

entities.name: Humpback dolphin
entities.fact: Humpback dolphins live in shallow coastal waters and estuaries and have a distinctive hump beneath the dorsal fin.

entities.name: Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin
entities.fact: Chinese white dolphins of the Pearl River estuary are actually pink as adults, and Hong Kong adopted them as its 1997 handover mascot.

entities.name: Atlantic humpback dolphin
entities.fact: The Atlantic humpback dolphin lives in estuaries and shallow coasts of West Africa and is critically endangered, with fewer than 3,000 left.

entities.name: Indian Ocean humpback dolphin
entities.fact: The Indian Ocean humpback dolphin has a pronounced hump under its dorsal fin and lives in estuaries and shallow coasts from South Africa to India.

entities.name: Australian humpback dolphin
entities.fact: The Australian humpback dolphin was described in 2014 and lives in shallow coastal waters and estuaries of northern Australia and New Guinea.

entities.name: Tucuxi
entities.fact: The tucuxi is a small grey dolphin that lives in the Amazon river system yet looks like a miniature bottlenose rather than a river dolphin.

entities.name: Guiana dolphin
entities.fact: The Guiana dolphin lives in estuaries and bays along the Atlantic coast of South and Central America and can sense electric fields with its snout.

entities.name: River dolphin
entities.fact: River dolphins have long slender beaks, tiny eyes and flexible necks suited to hunting in murky, cluttered water.

entities.name: Amazon river dolphin
entities.fact: The Amazon river dolphin turns pink with age and has an unfused neck that lets it turn its head to hunt among flooded trees.

entities.name: Bolivian river dolphin
entities.fact: The Bolivian river dolphin lives in the upper Madeira basin, cut off from the Amazon by rapids, and was declared part of Bolivia's natural heritage in 2012.

entities.name: Araguaian river dolphin
entities.fact: The Araguaian river dolphin of Brazil was described in 2014, the first new river dolphin species recognised in almost a century.

entities.name: Ganges river dolphin
entities.fact: The Ganges river dolphin is effectively blind, with eyes that lack a lens, and finds its way through muddy rivers by echolocation.

entities.name: Indus river dolphin
entities.fact: The Indus river dolphin often swims on its side in the shallow, muddy Indus and was long trapped between irrigation barrages.

entities.name: Baiji
entities.fact: The baiji of the Yangtze was declared functionally extinct in 2006 after a survey failed to find a single animal.

entities.name: Franciscana
entities.fact: The franciscana, or La Plata dolphin, lives in the Río de la Plata estuary and nearby coasts and has the longest beak for its size of any dolphin.

entities.name: Harbour porpoise
entities.fact: The harbour porpoise is the smallest cetacean in European waters and must feed almost constantly to stay warm.

entities.name: Vaquita
entities.fact: The vaquita, a tiny porpoise of the upper Gulf of California near the Colorado River delta, is the most endangered marine mammal, with perhaps only about 10 left.

entities.name: Dall's porpoise
entities.fact: Dall's porpoise is one of the fastest small cetaceans, throwing up a rooster tail of spray, and Japan's hunt of it is the largest direct hunt of any cetacean.

entities.name: Burmeister's porpoise
entities.fact: Burmeister's porpoise of South America is named after German zoologist Hermann Burmeister and has a strange backward-leaning dorsal fin.

entities.name: Spectacled porpoise
entities.fact: The spectacled porpoise has dark rings around its eyes like glasses and lives in cold sub-Antarctic waters, where it is rarely seen alive.

entities.name: Finless porpoise
entities.fact: Finless porpoises have no dorsal fin and live in shallow coastal waters, estuaries and rivers of Asia, including the Yangtze.

entities.name: Yangtze finless porpoise
entities.fact: The Yangtze finless porpoise is the only porpoise that lives entirely in fresh water and numbers only around a thousand.

entities.name: Indo-Pacific finless porpoise
entities.fact: The Indo-Pacific finless porpoise lives in estuaries and shallow coasts from the Persian Gulf to the Taiwan Strait, including the Pearl River estuary.

entities.name: Seal
entities.fact: Seals are marine mammals with streamlined bodies and flippers, and true seals have no external ear flaps.

entities.name: Harbour seal
entities.fact: Harbour seals are the most widespread pinniped, hauling out on coasts all around the Northern Hemisphere.

entities.name: Grey seal
entities.fact: Grey seal pups are born with white fur and are weaned in under three weeks, after which the mother leaves them to fend for themselves.

entities.name: Walrus
entities.fact: Walruses use their tusks to haul themselves onto ice, and a big male can weigh over 1,500 kilograms.

entities.name: Sea lion
entities.fact: Sea lions differ from true seals in having small external ear flaps and in walking on all four flippers on land.

entities.name: Elephant seal
entities.fact: Elephant seals are named for the huge inflatable nose of the males, which amplifies their roars during breeding fights.

entities.name: Northern elephant seal
entities.fact: Northern elephant seals were hunted to the brink of extinction in the 19th century, with perhaps fewer than 100 left, and now number well over 100,000.

entities.name: Southern elephant seal
entities.fact: The southern elephant seal is the largest seal and the largest carnivoran, with bulls weighing up to about 4 tonnes.

entities.name: Leopard seal
entities.fact: Leopard seals are the Antarctic's top seal predator, hunting penguins and the pups of other seals.

entities.name: Harp seal
entities.fact: Harp seal pups are born on the sea ice with fluffy white coats, and the species was the focus of the famous Canadian seal hunt protests.

entities.name: Hooded seal
entities.fact: Male hooded seals inflate a bright red nasal balloon from one nostril to impress rivals, and pups are weaned in only four days.

entities.name: Ringed seal
entities.fact: Ringed seals are the smallest and most common Arctic seal, keeping breathing holes open in the ice with their claws, and are the polar bear's main prey.

entities.name: Bearded seal
entities.fact: Bearded seals have long white whiskers for finding clams and crabs on the Arctic seabed, and males sing long trilling songs under the ice.

entities.name: Spotted seal
entities.fact: Spotted seals breed on the sea ice of the Bering and Okhotsk Seas and are closely related to harbour seals.

entities.name: Ribbon seal
entities.fact: Ribbon seals have striking white bands around the neck and flippers and spend most of the year in the open Bering Sea and Sea of Okhotsk.

entities.name: Weddell seal
entities.fact: Weddell seals live further south than any other mammal, under the fast ice of Antarctica, and can dive for over an hour.

entities.name: Crabeater seal
entities.fact: Crabeater seals do not eat crabs at all; they strain krill through their intricately lobed teeth and are probably the most numerous seal on Earth.

entities.name: Ross seal
entities.fact: The Ross seal is the least-known Antarctic seal, living deep in the pack ice and making eerie siren-like calls.

entities.name: Monk seal
entities.fact: Monk seals are the only seals adapted to warm tropical and subtropical waters, and only two species survive today.

entities.name: Hawaiian monk seal
entities.fact: The Hawaiian monk seal is one of the rarest seals, with only around 1,500 left, and its Hawaiian name means 'dog that runs in rough water'.

entities.name: Mediterranean monk seal
entities.fact: The Mediterranean monk seal gives birth in sea caves and numbers fewer than a thousand, most of them in Greece and off Mauritania.

entities.name: Caribbean monk seal
entities.fact: The Caribbean monk seal was hunted for its oil and was declared extinct in 2008, the last confirmed sighting having been in 1952.

entities.name: Caspian seal
entities.fact: The Caspian seal lives only in the landlocked Caspian Sea, where it breeds on winter ice in the north.

entities.name: Baikal seal
entities.fact: The Baikal seal lives only in Lake Baikal in Siberia and is the only seal that spends its whole life in fresh water.

entities.name: Fur seal
entities.fact: Fur seals have a dense double layer of fur that once made them a target for hunters, and they are more closely related to sea lions than to true seals.

entities.name: Northern fur seal
entities.fact: Most of the world's northern fur seals breed on the Pribilof Islands in the Bering Sea, where they were once hunted by the hundreds of thousands.

entities.name: Antarctic fur seal
entities.fact: Antarctic fur seals were nearly wiped out by 19th-century sealers but now breed by the millions on South Georgia.

entities.name: Cape fur seal
entities.fact: Cape fur seals breed in huge colonies on the coasts of South Africa and Namibia, where great whites ambush them at Seal Island.

entities.name: Galápagos fur seal
entities.fact: The Galápagos fur seal is the smallest fur seal and lives further north than any other, right on the equator.

entities.name: California sea lion
entities.fact: California sea lions are the trained 'seals' of circuses and aquarium shows and haul out in noisy crowds on San Francisco's Pier 39.

entities.name: Steller sea lion
entities.fact: Steller sea lions are the largest sea lions, with bulls reaching about a tonne, and are named after naturalist Georg Steller.

entities.name: Australian sea lion
entities.fact: The Australian sea lion is one of the rarest sea lions and has an unusual 17- to 18-month breeding cycle.

entities.name: Galápagos sea lion
entities.fact: Galápagos sea lions are so unafraid of people that they sleep on park benches and fish-market floors in the islands' towns.

entities.name: New Zealand sea lion
entities.fact: The New Zealand sea lion, or Hooker's sea lion, is one of the rarest sea lions and breeds mainly on the remote Auckland Islands.

entities.name: South American sea lion
entities.fact: South American sea lion males have a huge mane-like neck that earned the species its 'lion' name, and some hunt penguins and fur seal pups.

entities.name: Sea otter
entities.fact: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal and use rocks as tools to crack open shellfish.

entities.name: Marine otter
entities.fact: The marine otter, or chungungo, of Chile and Peru is the smallest marine mammal, weighing about 4 kilograms, and lives along rocky shores.

entities.name: Manatee
entities.fact: Manatees are gentle plant-eaters whose closest living relatives on land are elephants.

entities.name: West Indian manatee
entities.fact: West Indian manatees crowd into Florida's warm springs in winter because they cannot survive long in water below about 20 degrees Celsius.

entities.name: West African manatee
entities.fact: The West African manatee lives in coastal lagoons and rivers from Senegal to Angola and is the least-studied of the sirenians.

entities.name: Dugong
entities.fact: Dugongs graze on seagrass meadows and have a fluked tail like a whale's, unlike the manatee's rounded paddle.

entities.name: Steller's sea cow
entities.fact: Steller's sea cow, an 8-metre relative of the dugong, was hunted to extinction within about 27 years of its discovery in 1741.

entities.name: Polar bear
entities.fact: Polar bears are classed as marine mammals because they spend most of their lives on sea ice hunting seals, and they can swim for days.

entities.name: Greenland shark
entities.fact: Greenland sharks grow about a centimetre a year and may live for several centuries, longer than any other known vertebrate.

entities.name: Pacific sleeper shark
entities.fact: The Pacific sleeper shark is a sluggish giant of cold northern waters that has been recorded at depths of around 2,000 metres.

entities.name: Greenland halibut
entities.fact: The Greenland halibut's migrating eye stops at the top edge of its head, so it can swim upright as well as lie flat.

entities.name: Arctic cod
entities.fact: Arctic cod carry antifreeze proteins in their blood and live right under the sea ice, feeding seals, whales and seabirds.

entities.name: Arctic char
entities.fact: Arctic char live further north than any other freshwater fish, and sea-run char feed in Arctic coastal waters each summer.

entities.name: Capelin
entities.fact: Capelin are small silvery fish that spawn on Arctic and sub-Arctic beaches in their millions and feed cod, whales and puffins.

entities.name: Atlantic wolffish
entities.fact: The Atlantic wolffish produces antifreeze proteins to survive icy Arctic water and crushes sea urchins and crabs with its canine-like teeth.

entities.name: Arctic skate
entities.fact: The Arctic skate lives on deep, cold seabeds across the Arctic basin and lays its eggs in tough leathery cases.

entities.name: Lion's mane jellyfish
entities.fact: The lion's mane jellyfish of cold northern seas is the largest known jellyfish, with tentacles that can trail over 30 metres.

entities.name: Sea angel
entities.fact: The sea angel is a tiny swimming sea slug of Arctic waters that flaps two wing-like lobes and preys only on sea butterflies.

entities.name: Sea butterfly
entities.fact: Sea butterflies are tiny swimming snails that flap wing-like flaps, and their thin shells are threatened by ocean acidification.

entities.name: Snow crab
entities.fact: Snow crabs live on cold northern seabeds, and billions vanished from the Bering Sea after a marine heatwave, closing the fishery in 2022.

entities.name: Northern shrimp
entities.fact: Northern shrimp start life as males and change into females as they age, and they are the main cold-water prawn on sale in Europe.

entities.name: Atlantic puffin
entities.fact: Atlantic puffins can carry a dozen or more small fish crosswise in their beaks at once and spend the winter alone far out at sea.

entities.name: Arctic tern
entities.fact: The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, the longest migration of any animal, around 70,000 kilometres or more.

entities.name: Ivory gull
entities.fact: The ivory gull is a pure-white gull that lives year-round among Arctic pack ice and scavenges polar bear kills.

entities.name: Little auk
entities.fact: The little auk is one of the most numerous seabirds in the Arctic, breeding in colonies of millions in Greenland and Svalbard.

entities.name: Thick-billed murre
entities.fact: Thick-billed murres dive deeper than any other flying bird, to over 200 metres, in Arctic and sub-Arctic seas.

entities.name: Sea turtle
entities.fact: Sea turtles cannot pull their heads into their shells, and females return to the beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.

entities.name: Green sea turtle
entities.fact: Green sea turtles are named for the green fat under their shells, a result of their diet of seagrass and algae.

entities.name: Leatherback sea turtle
entities.fact: The leatherback is the largest turtle, can weigh over 600 kilograms, and dives to over 1,000 metres hunting jellyfish.

entities.name: Hawksbill sea turtle
entities.fact: Hawksbills eat sea sponges that are toxic to most animals, and their patterned shells were the source of 'tortoiseshell'.

entities.name: Loggerhead sea turtle
entities.fact: Loggerheads have massive jaws for crushing clams and crabs and migrate across the whole Pacific from Japan to Mexico.

entities.name: Kemp's ridley sea turtle
entities.fact: Kemp's ridley is the rarest sea turtle and nests in mass daytime arrivals called arribadas, mostly on one Mexican beach, Rancho Nuevo.

entities.name: Olive ridley sea turtle
entities.fact: Olive ridleys nest in arribadas of tens of thousands of females on single beaches in Costa Rica, Mexico and India.

entities.name: Flatback sea turtle
entities.fact: The flatback sea turtle nests only in Australia and has a flattened shell with upturned edges.

entities.name: Saltwater crocodile
entities.fact: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, over 6 metres long, and swims between islands across hundreds of kilometres of open sea.

entities.name: American crocodile
entities.fact: American crocodiles live in coastal mangroves and lagoons from Florida to Peru and have salt glands that let them tolerate the sea.

entities.name: Marine iguana
entities.fact: The marine iguana of the Galápagos is the only lizard that feeds in the sea, grazing algae underwater and sneezing out salt.

entities.name: Sea snake
entities.fact: Sea snakes are venomous relatives of cobras with paddle-shaped tails, and most give birth to live young at sea.

entities.name: Sea krait
entities.fact: Sea kraits are the only sea snakes that come ashore to lay eggs, and they have highly potent venom but rarely bite people.

entities.name: Yellow-bellied sea snake
entities.fact: The yellow-bellied sea snake is the most widespread snake on Earth, drifting across the Pacific and Indian Oceans and never coming ashore.

entities.name: Banded sea krait
entities.fact: Banded sea kraits hunt eels on reefs but return to land to digest their meals, shed their skins and lay eggs.

entities.name: Olive sea snake
entities.fact: The olive sea snake of Australian reefs has light-sensing cells in its tail, so it can keep its tail hidden in a crevice.

entities.name: Beaked sea snake
entities.fact: The beaked sea snake causes most sea snake bites and deaths, especially among fishermen pulling nets in South and Southeast Asia.

entities.name: Stokes's sea snake
entities.fact: Stokes's sea snake is one of the heaviest sea snakes, with a thick body and the longest fangs of any sea snake.

entities.name: Turtle-headed sea snake
entities.fact: The turtle-headed sea snake has almost no teeth and feeds only on fish eggs, which it scrapes from the reef.

entities.name: Dubois' sea snake
entities.fact: Dubois' sea snake of northern Australia is among the most venomous snakes known, yet it is placid and feeds on small reef fish.

entities.name: Elegant sea snake
entities.fact: The elegant sea snake is one of the longest sea snakes, reaching about 2 metres, and lives in the turbid waters off northern Australia.

entities.name: Horned sea snake
entities.fact: The horned sea snake has small spines over its eyes and is the only sea snake with spiny scales on its head.

entities.name: Black-banded sea krait
entities.fact: The black-banded sea krait, or erabu, is caught and smoked in Okinawa to make a traditional soup called irabu-jiru.

entities.name: Spine-bellied sea snake
entities.fact: The spine-bellied sea snake is a stout, aggressive sea snake often caught in trawl nets off Australia and Southeast Asia.

entities.name: Annulated sea snake
entities.fact: The annulated sea snake can take in oxygen through a network of blood vessels on top of its head, which works a little like a snorkel.

entities.name: Blue-lipped sea krait
entities.fact: The blue-lipped sea krait comes ashore on Pacific and Indian Ocean islands to rest and lay its eggs in caves and crevices.

entities.name: Leaf-scaled sea snake
entities.fact: The leaf-scaled sea snake vanished from Ashmore Reef and was feared extinct until it turned up again off Western Australia in 2015.

entities.name: Belcher's sea snake
entities.fact: Belcher's sea snake is often wrongly called the world's most venomous snake; its venom is potent, but it is docile and rarely bites.

entities.name: Ornate sea snake
entities.fact: The ornate sea snake lives on reefs and sandy flats around northern Australia and feeds on fish and fish eggs.

entities.name: Short-nosed sea snake
entities.fact: The short-nosed sea snake was feared extinct for 15 years until a pair was photographed courting on Ningaloo Reef in 2015.

entities.name: Crab
entities.fact: Crabs must shed their hard shells to grow, hiding away while the soft new shell underneath hardens.

entities.name: Lobster
entities.fact: Lobsters keep growing throughout their lives by moulting their shells, and some may live for decades.

entities.name: Clam
entities.fact: Clams pull themselves through sand with a muscular foot and draw in water through a siphon to filter out food.

entities.name: Oyster
entities.fact: A single oyster can filter up to around 190 litres of water a day, and oyster reefs once lined estuaries such as New York Harbour.

entities.name: Mussel
entities.fact: Mussels anchor themselves to rocks with tough byssal threads, which have inspired new surgical glues.

entities.name: Scallop
entities.fact: Scallops have dozens of tiny blue eyes along the edge of their shells and can swim by clapping their shells together.

entities.name: Barnacle
entities.fact: Barnacles are crustaceans, relatives of crabs, that glue their heads to rocks and build limestone shells around themselves.

entities.name: Shrimp
entities.fact: Shrimps and prawns wear a thin, flexible shell that they shed many times as they grow.

entities.name: Sea urchin
entities.fact: A sea urchin's spines sit on a rigid shell called a test, which is made of plates of calcium carbonate.

entities.name: Abalone
entities.fact: Abalone shells are lined with iridescent mother-of-pearl and have a row of holes through which the animal breathes.

entities.name: Conch
entities.fact: The queen conch builds a heavy pink-lipped shell and hops along the seabed by pole-vaulting on a claw-like foot.

entities.name: Cowrie
entities.fact: Cowrie shells stay smooth and glossy because the living animal wraps its mantle over the outside, and they once served as money across Africa and Asia.

entities.name: Horseshoe crab
entities.fact: Horseshoe crabs have blue, copper-based blood that is harvested to test medicines and vaccines for bacterial contamination.

entities.name: Giant clam
entities.fact: Giant clams can grow over a metre across and get much of their food from algae living in their colourful mantle tissue.

entities.name: Hermit crab
entities.fact: Hermit crabs have soft abdomens and move into empty snail shells, swapping for larger ones as they grow.

entities.name: Nautilus
entities.fact: The nautilus controls its buoyancy by adjusting gas in the chambers of its spiral shell, and its lineage has changed little in hundreds of millions of years.

entities.name: Sea snail
entities.fact: Sea snails build their spiral shells from calcium carbonate drawn from seawater, adding to the opening as they grow.

entities.name: Limpet
entities.fact: Limpets clamp their cone-shaped shells to rocks and return to the exact same 'home scar' after every grazing trip.

entities.name: Whelk
entities.fact: Common whelks are scavenging and predatory sea snails of the North Atlantic, and their spongy egg masses wash up as 'sea wash balls'.

entities.name: Periwinkle
entities.fact: Periwinkles are small shore snails that seal themselves inside their shells with a trapdoor to survive hours out of water at low tide.

entities.name: Cockle
entities.fact: Cockles live buried just under the sand of tidal flats and can leap away from predators by flexing their foot.

entities.name: King crab
entities.fact: Red king crabs of the Bering Sea can span 1.5 metres across the legs and are actually closer relatives of hermit crabs than of true crabs.

entities.name: Spiny lobster
entities.fact: Spiny lobsters have no big claws and march across the seabed in single-file lines of dozens during autumn migrations.

entities.name: Chiton
entities.fact: Chitons wear a shell of eight overlapping plates and can roll into a ball like a woodlouse when prised from a rock.

entities.name: Argonaut
entities.fact: The female argonaut, an octopus, secretes a thin, papery shell that she uses as a floating egg case and buoyancy aid.

entities.name: Sand dollar
entities.fact: Sand dollars are flattened sea urchins, and the bleached white 'shell' found on beaches is the animal's skeleton, or test.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck's siphon is so long that it cannot fit inside its shell, and the clam can live for over 150 years buried in the seabed.

entities.name: Tusk shell
entities.fact: Tusk shells are molluscs with a tapering tubular shell open at both ends, living head-down in sand.

entities.name: Cone snail
entities.fact: Cone snails fire a venomous harpoon from their beautiful shells, and a few species can kill a person.

entities.name: Triton's trumpet
entities.fact: The Triton's trumpet is a huge sea snail that preys on crown-of-thorns starfish, and its shell has been blown as a horn for centuries.

entities.name: Ocean quahog
entities.fact: An ocean quahog dredged up off Iceland in 2006 was 507 years old, the oldest known individual animal ever found.

entities.name: Razor clam
entities.fact: Razor clams can dig down through wet sand faster than a person can dig, which is why collectors sprinkle salt to make them pop up.

entities.name: Ram's horn squid
entities.fact: The ram's horn squid carries a coiled, chambered shell inside its body, and the little white shells wash up on beaches worldwide.
